newsitem.title: PERU: Key Peru hostage crisis meeting falls apart.
newsitem.headline: Key Peru hostage crisis meeting falls apart.

text.p: A much-anticipated meeting between Peru's chief negotiator and Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence collapsed before it began on Sunday, dashing hopes of an end to the 26-day crisis any time soon.

Education Minister and chief negotiator Domingo Palermo told a news conference the planned meeting was called off after the rebels told him it could only take place if he took with him a proposal to free some 400 jailed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
"If I did not, it was preferable not to meet, as there was no possibility of talking," Palermo told a news conference. "I really regret this."
Peru's President, Alberto Fujimori, has ruled out freeing any jailed MRTA members, whose release is the main rebel demand.
Palermo said he had sent a counterproposal to Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, head of the MRTA rebels in the residence, outlining the government's conditions for resuming talks.

These included the establishment of a "guarantor commission" made up of representatives from the government, the MRTA, the Vatican and the International Committee of the Red Cross. Members would jointly seek a peaceful end to the standoff.
"This proposal has the healthy intention of facilitating the peaceful outcome we all wish for," Palermo's note to Cerpa said. A copy of the proposal was made available to reporters.
"We understand that it is necessary to establish this framework, which may naturally be modified with any suggestions that may be considered suitable."
Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who has visited the residence regularly throughout the crisis, had been named the Vatican's representative to the commission, Palermo said.

Sunday's meeting, arranged in a walkie-talkie conversation between Palermo and Cerpa on Friday, would have been their second face-to-face encounter since the rebels stormed a diplomatic reception on Dec. 17, taking more than 500 hostages.
The two men had not met since holding talks inside the residence on Dec. 28 after which 20 hostages were freed. They have since exchanged several written messages.
Palermo said he would no longer be in radio contact with Cerpa, at the request of the rebels, because a reporter had leaked a tape recording of their complete Friday conversation.

He said he was still in touch via other confidential means and was sending his proposal to the rebels via Michel Minnig, the chief representative of the Red Cross in Peru, who has been a key go-between for the two sides.
Of the hundreds of hostages it took, the MRTA has released the majority in what it has called "goodwill gestures."
The 74 captives left include dozens of Peruvian officials and Japanese businessmen as well as Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro, and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.

In New York, A Japanese TV reporter who sneaked into the residence last week and was then arrested and held by Peruvian antiterrorist police for four days apologised to the families of the hostages for his action.

"I do apologise for causing worry to the families of the hostages and the International Red Cross workers and others," Tsuyoshi Hitomi, a journalist with a subsidiary of Japan's TV Asahi, told a news conference after arriving from Peru.

Peru and Japan were infuriated by Hitoshi and his Peruvian interpreter, saying they, and a previous impromptu press conference in the residence, set back talks and prevented the release of more hostages by denying the government the bargaining chip of deciding when to grant the MRTA publicity.

In another apparent breach of security at the siege site on Sunday, two photographers -- identified as employees of the Peruvian investigative magazine Caretas -- hoisted themselves onto a garden wall at the rear of the besieged compound and took photographs from about 50 yards (meters).

Thousands of Peruvians from Lima's shantytowns converged behind the security cordon around the residence and appealed to the guerrillas to free their captives. The protesters voiced strong support for Fujimori's tough line.
"Support for Fujimori. Do not give in to terrorists," the crowd chanted.
